gtlcore.quest.gtl.quest.010cf028448c17a9: Of course, voltages can be converted using Transformers. A Transformer can only convert between two adjacent voltage tiers, and has both step-up and step-down modes. In step-up mode, 1 voltage tier and 4x current are converted into 1 tier higher voltage and 1x current; step-down mode is the reverse.

There are four types of Transformers: Normal, Adjustable (2A), 4A, and 16A (Hi-Amp) Transformers. Normal is 1A<-->4A, 2A is 2A<-->8A, 4A is 4A<-->16A, and 16A is 16A<-->64A. The red side of a Transformer corresponds to low voltage, and the green side corresponds to high voltage.

The multiblock Active Transformer unlocked in LuV supports mutual conversion between any voltage and any amperage, automatically stepping up or down, and can replace all regular Transformers in mid-to-late-game high-voltage, high-amperage setups.
However, the real use of the Active Transformer is bending laser beams.

gtlcore.quest.gtl.quest.0cc922b821305906: In GregTech, electricity is transmitted in "packets". The size of each packet corresponds to its voltage tier.
Take an LV packet for example: this "packet" carries 32EU. Multiple blocks can produce these EU packets, and packets are only generated when a destination is reachable.
Every tick (1/20 second, or 0.05 seconds), EU "packets" attempt to transfer from energy producers to consumers.
These "packets" have two parameters: the voltage tier (V) determined by the producer's tier, and the amperage (A), which determines how much power can actually be transferred.
Energy is only transferred when a full amp "packet" can be received. You may notice your machines sitting just below full EU capacity - they only accept EU when missing at least 1A of input voltage.
If a machine receives a voltage higher than its voltage tier, it will explode, but any excess amperage has no adverse effect because machines only draw what they need.
Machine explosions normally destroy terrain as well, but this feature is disabled in this pack.
In short, energy is transferred in "packets": 32EU for LV, 128EU for MV... and so on. Due to cable loss, the energy actually received by a machine may be lower than the energy sent.
Machine energy input is limited by both voltage and amperage; therefore, an MV machine connected to an LV line with 1A input will never accept more than 32EU/t of power.

You can still run an MV machine on an LV line, but only if the recipe power is low enough, or if you have an MV battery in the machine's battery slot—when idle, the machine will only accept 1A, charging the battery at a maximum rate of 32EU/t.

Wrench:
When holding a Wrench and looking at a wrenchable block, a 3x3 grid appears on the block face:
The center section is largest, the edges are medium, and the corners are smallest.

Right-clicking the center of a machine face rotates the front face to that side (for non-GT machines with a front face) or sets the output face to that side (for GT machines); right-clicking an edge rotates the face toward that edge's direction; right-clicking a corner rotates the face to the opposite side. If right-clicking a non-directional non-GT machine, all of these actions dismantle the machine. Shift + Right-Clicking the center rotates the front face to that side (for all machines), and edges/corners behave the same way. For non-directional non-GT machines, this also dismantles the machine.

Right-clicking the center of a pipe face does nothing; right-clicking an edge connects/disconnects the pipe in that edge's direction; right-clicking a corner connects/disconnects the pipe on the opposite side. Shift + Right-Clicking toggles whether input is blocked from that side.

Right-clicking any non-front face of Logs, Hay Bales, Comparators, Repeaters, Pumpkins, Jack o'Lanterns, Pistons, Sticky Pistons, Droppers, Dispensers, Furnaces, Chests, Trapped Chests, Ender Chests, or Hoppers rotates them;

Right-clicking the front face of Crafting Tables, Bookshelves, Pumpkins, Jack o'Lanterns, Pistons, Sticky Pistons, Droppers, Dispensers, Furnaces, Chests, Trapped Chests, Ender Chests, or Hoppers dismantles them.
In addition to these, blocks like Levers and Rails can also be rotated or dismantled.

Screwdriver:
Used to configure output faces and craft components.
Right-clicking a machine's front face or output face toggles whether input is allowed through the output face.

More accurately: if the face corresponding to the 3x3 grid section can be configured by a Screwdriver, it configures that face directly; otherwise, it has no effect. The grid mapping follows the same rules as the Wrench.

An Electric Motor is a device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. Its operation is based on electromagnetic induction: when current flows through the motor's coil, a force is generated in the magnetic field, causing the rotor to spin and drive a load. Electric Motors are widely used across industrial, commercial, and household appliances.

An Electric Piston is an electrically driven reciprocating device that converts the rotational motion of an electric motor into linear back-and-forth motion. Such devices are used in various applications like compressors, pneumatic actuators, and robot arms.

A Robot Arm is a mechanical device that mimics the function of a human arm, typically consisting of a series of links and joints capable of complex movements including rotation, bending, and extension. Robot Arms can be programmed or remotely controlled to perform tasks such as handling, assembly, welding, spraying, measurement, and exploration.

A Conveyor Module is a transport mechanism used to move materials or products from one place to another. It consists of one or more continuous belts rotating around two pulleys that serve as drive and support points. Conveyors can run horizontally, at an incline, or vertically to suit different transport needs.

gtlcore.quest.gtl.quest.6f503441c24abd5b: Running 16 LV machines simultaneously uses the same power as a single HV machine, but is four times as fast. This is because the 16 LV machines do not suffer the efficiency loss from imperfect overclocking, allowing them to get more done despite running slower individually.
Multiblock parallelism is a similar concept. Simply put, parallelism is an alternative form of perfect overclocking.
Sub-tick parallelism (1toc) is a mechanic triggered by certain multiblocks when processing a single recipe takes less than 1 game tick.
No singleblock machines or cross-recipe parallel machines will trigger 1toc.

Example 1: When a LuV-tier multiblock processes an IV-tier recipe that takes exactly 1 game tick, it will process 2 recipes per game tick; if the machine's voltage tier is one tier higher (reaching ZPM), it will process 4 recipes per game tick. If the machine has perfect overclocking (such as the Large Chemical Reactor), it will process 4 and 16 recipes in parallel at LuV and ZPM respectively.

Example 2: For a recipe that takes 3 game ticks with perfect overclocking (each overclock tier reduces duration to 1/4 while keeping total energy cost unchanged), overclocking by one tier will process 4 recipes simultaneously while keeping the duration at 3 game ticks.
Cross-recipe parallelism is a mechanic exclusive to certain multiblock machines, allowing the machine to execute multiple different recipes under the same machine mode simultaneously.
Correspondingly, the minimum duration for cross-recipe parallel machines is 1 second
Example: The Holy Separator can craft Silver Rods and Iron Rods simultaneously, but cannot centrifuge Air and craft Iron Rods at the same time.

"Threads" is a unique attribute of machines with cross-recipe parallelism (all have 64 threads). The total parallelism of a cross-recipe parallel machine equals the thread count multiplied by the machine's own parallelism, and the thread count represents the maximum number of recipes the total parallelism can be distributed across. Note: Cross-recipe parallel machines will allocate as much of their total parallelism as possible to a single recipe.

The formula for calculating the time taken by a machine under cross-parallel operation is: total energy consumption divided by input power. Unlike the discrete time variations seen in non-cross-parallel operations, cross-parallel operation is equivalent to continuous, lossless overclocking.
